title: 2010 audio recording on alleged undeclared Smer financing
description: Shortly before the June 2010 parliamentary election, the daily Sme published an anonymously supplied audio recording in which a voice strongly resembling Fico's talks about having secured money for Smer from undisclosed sponsors, bypassing the party's official accounts, in the period before the 2002 election. Fico called the recording a fake ('I can produce as many such recordings as I want'), described it as part of an anti-campaign, announced legal action against Sme's editor-in-chief and told journalists at a press conference: 'Now you all will be jerking off about it; I wish you a pleasant sexual experience' (Slovak Spectator). KDH MP Daniel Lipšic passed the recording to the Prosecutor General's Office. In December 2010 the criminal inquiry into Smer's financing was halted by the prosecutor handling it, amid a public dispute between Prosecutor General Dobroslav Trnka and Interior Minister Lipšic over alleged pressure on the investigator, who said she had not been pressured. The authenticity of the recording was never established and no one was charged.
key_facts: Recording published by Sme in June 2010, two days before the election
Fico said it was fake and part of an 'anti-campaign'; he used vulgar language towards journalists about it
Inquiry into Smer financing halted in December 2010; no charges

title: Suspensions of Smer by the Party of European Socialists (2006, 2023) and expulsion (2025)
description: On 12 October 2006 the Party of European Socialists (PES) suspended Smer for forming a government with Ján Slota's Slovak National Party (SNS), citing its founding principle against cooperation with nationalist and xenophobic parties; Fico's spokesperson said Smer was being punished for 'doing politics for the people' (Slovak Spectator). Smer was later readmitted and became a full member in 2009. After the 2023 election, in which Smer again formed a coalition including the SNS, the PES suspended Smer and Hlas in October 2023 over a 'clear divergence from the values' of the PES, citing their positions on Russia's war against Ukraine, migration, the rule of law and LGBTIQ people (STVR Radio Slovakia International). In October 2025 the PES expelled Smer in a unanimous decision for 'breaching the values' of the party family; Fico criticised the PES for abandoning authentic left-wing values and said Smer had received offers from other European Parliament groups, including talks with Viktor Orbán about the Patriots for Europe (Euronews).
key_facts: 12 October 2006: PES suspends Smer over its coalition with the SNS
October 2023: PES suspends Smer and Hlas
October 2025: PES expels Smer unanimously

title: Insults directed at journalists and the 2023 boycott of four media outlets
description: Fico has repeatedly used insulting language about journalists. On 23 November 2016, asked about alleged irregularities in contracts linked to Slovakia's EU Council presidency, he told reporters: 'You are fighting against this government. Some of you are dirty anti-Slovak prostitutes. I stand by my words'; the Slovak section of the Association of European Journalists asked him to apologise (STVR Radio Slovakia International, Euronews). OCCRP noted in 2018 that he had previously called journalists 'prostitutes', 'dirt' and 'idiots'. On 20 November 2023, a month after returning to office, he announced in a letter that he was cutting off communication with TV Markíza, Denník N, Sme and Aktuality.sk until they 'fulfil their legal obligations' to inform the public truthfully, after earlier calling them 'hostile' media; journalism students protested outside the Government Office (STVR Radio Slovakia International). In January 2024 the European Parliament regretted the decision of Fico and government officials to stop talking to key outlets and demanded an end to verbal attacks on media representatives.
key_facts: 23 November 2016: 'dirty anti-Slovak prostitutes' remark; journalists' association demanded an apology
20 November 2023: communication cut off with Markíza, Denník N, Sme and Aktuality.sk
17 January 2024: European Parliament resolution criticises the boycott and verbal attacks on media

title: Renting a flat in the Bonaparte complex from businessman Ladislav Bašternák
description: For about seven years Fico rented a large flat in the Bonaparte residential complex near Bratislava Castle owned by businessman Ladislav Bašternák. In March 2017 police charged Bašternák with tax offences over a VAT refund of about €1.97 million claimed in 2012; the case became one of the main scandals of Fico's third government, and links were alleged between Bašternák and Interior Minister Robert Kaliňák. According to the Slovak Spectator, Fico had said in February 2017 that he would leave the flat immediately if Bašternák were charged, but did not do so at the time. Bašternák was later convicted of tax fraud and his property forfeited; Fico moved out in the summer of 2019 and the flat was auctioned by the bankruptcy trustee. Fico was not accused of any offence in connection with the tenancy.
key_facts: Fico rented the Bonaparte flat from Bašternák from 2012
Bašternák charged in March 2017 over a VAT refund of more than €1.97 million; later convicted
Fico moved out in summer 2019 after the property was forfeited

title: Opposition to EU refugee relocation quotas and statements on Islam (2015–2017)
description: During the 2015 refugee crisis Fico's government opposed the EU's mandatory relocation of asylum seekers and, with Hungary, brought an action at the EU Court of Justice against the Council decision of September 2015. In a May 2016 interview with the TASR agency, shortly before Slovakia's EU Council presidency, Fico said: 'There is no room for Islam in Slovakia', adding that those who say Slovakia wants to be multicultural are 'against the country in general' (STVR Radio Slovakia International). On 6 September 2017 the Court of Justice dismissed the Slovak and Hungarian actions (joined cases C-643/15 and C-647/15); Fico said Slovakia would respect the ruling but that the government's political position would not change.
key_facts: Slovakia sued the Council over the September 2015 relocation decision
May 2016: 'There is no room for Islam in Slovakia'
6 September 2017: Court of Justice dismissed the actions of Slovakia and Hungary

title: Murder of journalist Ján Kuciak and Martina Kušnírová (2018), the political crisis and Fico's resignation
description: Ján Kuciak, a 27-year-old investigative reporter at the news site Aktuality.sk who covered tax fraud, corruption and organised crime (notably the businessman Marian Kočner), and his fiancée Martina Kušnírová, also 27, were shot dead in their house in Veľká Mača (Galanta district) on 21 February 2018; the killings became public on 26 February. On 28 February Aktuality.sk and partner outlets, including OCCRP, published his unfinished last story on Italian businessmen with alleged links to the Calabrian 'Ndrangheta who had settled in eastern Slovakia, drew EU agricultural subsidies and had contacts with people in the Government Office, among them Mária Trošková, chief state adviser to Prime Minister Fico, and Viliam Jasaň, secretary of the State Security Council. At a press conference on 27 February Fico, with Interior Minister Robert Kaliňák and Police President Tibor Gašpar, displayed €1 million in cash offered for information on the killers, and said: 'You are connecting innocent people with double murder. That is over the line'; the next day he accused the opposition of abusing the murder, saying its 'only objective is to criminalise Smer and the whole government' (Slovak Spectator). On 28 February Trošková and Jasaň left their posts until the investigation was over, rejecting any link to the crime, and Culture Minister Marek Maďarič (Smer) resigned, saying he could not accept that a journalist had been killed during his tenure. After President Andrej Kiska called on 4 March for a broad government reshuffle or early elections, Fico on 5 March questioned Kiska's September 2017 meeting with George Soros in New York and suggested an attempt to destabilise the country; Soros's spokesman said Soros had played no role in Kiska's speech or the protests. The 'Za slušné Slovensko' ('For a Decent Slovakia') protests drew more than 100,000 people in Slovakia and abroad on 9 March and about 65,000 in Bratislava on 16 March (Slovak Spectator), described by Al Jazeera as the country's biggest demonstrations since 1989; according to OCCRP, Fico claimed they were part of a plot against him. Kaliňák resigned on 12 March after the junior coalition party Most-Híd demanded it. On 15 March 2018 President Kiska accepted the resignation of Fico and his government; Fico said a new government rather than early elections was 'the right step' and that he would remain an active party leader, and Deputy Prime Minister Peter Pellegrini (Smer) formed a new cabinet with the same coalition, appointed on 22 March. The European Parliament sent a fact-finding delegation of its civil liberties (LIBE) and budgetary control (CONT) committees to Slovakia on 8–9 March 2018 and on 19 April 2018 adopted a resolution (573 votes to 27, 47 abstentions) condemning the murders, calling for an independent investigation with a Europol-led joint team and noting the delegation's findings that the selection of top prosecutors was believed to be highly politicised. In the criminal proceedings, intermediary Zoltán Andruskó was sentenced to 15 years under a plea agreement (30 December 2019); gunman Miroslav Marček confessed and was sentenced to 23 years (6 April 2020), raised on appeal to a final 25 years by the Supreme Court (2 December 2020); and Tomáš Szabó, described by prosecutors as the driver, was sentenced to 25 years by the Specialised Criminal Court in Pezinok on 3 September 2020, a sentence the Supreme Court upheld on 15 June 2021. Prosecutors accuse Marian Kočner of ordering the murder through his associate Alena Zsuzsová; both contest the charges (Kočner told the court in 2020: 'I'm not a saint, but I'm not a murderer either'). The Specialised Criminal Court acquitted both on 3 September 2020; the Supreme Court annulled the acquittals on 15 June 2021; in the retrial (joined with the case of planned murders of prosecutors) the court again acquitted Kočner on 19 May 2023 and convicted Zsuzsová (25 years); on 20 May 2025 the Supreme Court (senate of Judge Peter Paluda, by two votes to one, in a non-public session) annulled that verdict, citing, according to its spokesperson, unclear factual findings, failure to take all necessary evidence and failure to address all relevant circumstances, and assigned the case to a different panel because the earlier binding instruction of the Supreme Court had not been followed. The third trial before a new panel of the Specialised Criminal Court began on 26 January 2026, with 42 hearing days scheduled through the end of 2026; as of October 2026 it was still hearing witnesses and no verdict had been delivered. Kočner and Zsuzsová are presumed innocent of the Kuciak murders, as neither has a final conviction in this case. Robert Fico was never charged, named as a suspect or implicated in the murder by investigators or courts, and is not a party to these proceedings, whose defendants are listed above; the record is therefore a public controversy over his government's handling of the crisis, not a legal case against him.
key_facts: Victims: Ján Kuciak, 27, investigative reporter at Aktuality.sk, and his fiancée Martina Kušnírová, 27; shot at home in Veľká Mača on 21 February 2018 (TASR, OCCRP).

Kuciak's unfinished last article, published posthumously on 28 February 2018 by Aktuality.sk and OCCRP, concerned 'Ndrangheta-linked Italian businessmen in eastern Slovakia, EU agricultural subsidies and their contacts in the Government Office (European Parliament summary, OCCRP).
27 February 2018: Fico, Kaliňák and Gašpar displayed €1 million in cash as a reward for information; Fico defended Trošková and Jasaň (Slovak Spectator).
28 February 2018: Trošková and Jasaň left the Government Office pending the investigation; Culture Minister Marek Maďarič resigned (Slovak Spectator).
5 March 2018: Fico raised President Kiska's 2017 meeting with George Soros; Soros denied any role in Kiska's speech or the protests (Slovak Spectator).

8–9 March 2018: European Parliament LIBE/CONT fact-finding delegation in Slovakia (STVR Radio Slovakia International); 19 April 2018: EP resolution adopted 573–27–47 (European Parliament Legislative Observatory).
'For a Decent Slovakia' protests: more than 100,000 people on 9 March 2018, about 65,000 in Bratislava on 16 March (Slovak Spectator).
12 March 2018: Interior Minister Robert Kaliňák resigned; 15 March 2018: President Kiska accepted Fico's resignation and asked Peter Pellegrini to form a government (Al Jazeera, OCCRP).
Final sentences: Andruskó 15 years (30 December 2019), Marček 25 years (Supreme Court, 2 December 2020), Szabó 25 years (upheld by the Supreme Court on 15 June 2021) (TASR, Slovak Spectator).

Kočner acquitted by the Specialised Criminal Court on 3 September 2020 and 19 May 2023; both verdicts annulled by the Supreme Court (15 June 2021, 20 May 2025); Zsuzsová's 2023 conviction also annulled (Slovak Spectator, SME).
Third trial before a new panel of the Specialised Criminal Court since 26 January 2026; hearings continuing in October 2026, no verdict (OCCRP, SME).
Fico was not charged or named as a suspect and is not a party to the murder proceedings.

title: Candidacy for the Constitutional Court (2019)
description: Ten months after resigning as Prime Minister, Fico was nominated in January 2019 by Smer MP Martin Glváč as a candidate for judge of the Constitutional Court, where nine of the thirteen seats were about to fall vacant; Glváč said Fico could become a good chairman of the court. On 12 February 2019, as parliament repeatedly failed to elect candidates in public votes, Fico withdrew, saying the new judges should be appointed by a new president (Slovak Spectator).
key_facts: Nominated in January 2019 by Smer MP Martin Glváč
Withdrew on 12 February 2019

title: Accusations against President Zuzana Čaputová ('American agent')
description: While in opposition, Fico repeatedly accused President Zuzana Čaputová of acting in the interest of the United States and of George Soros, according to her statements quoted by the Slovak Spectator. After she appointed a caretaker government in May 2023, he called the move 'anti-democratic' and the designated Prime Minister Ľudovít Ódor 'Soros's pick'. On 10 May 2023 Čaputová said Fico had 'again spread lies about me being an American agent', noted that she had attended hearings over new death threats against her and her family, and announced legal action; she also said courts had found such accusations unfounded, and in March 2022 a Bratislava court had ordered Smer MP Ľuboš Blaha to stop calling her a traitor and an agent of foreign countries (Slovak Spectator). Her civil lawsuit against Fico is listed in the justice section.
key_facts: Fico repeatedly linked Čaputová to the US and George Soros
May 2023: Čaputová announced legal action against Fico over the 'American agent' claims
Court order of March 2022 against Smer MP Ľuboš Blaha over similar claims

title: Abolition of the Special Prosecutor's Office and the 2024 criminal-law overhaul
description: On 6 December 2023 Fico's government launched a fast-tracked overhaul of criminal law that reduced penalties for several offences, shortened limitation periods and abolished the Special Prosecutor's Office, which had handled serious crime and high-profile corruption cases, including cases of people linked to the ruling parties; parliament passed it on 8 February 2024. According to the Slovak Spectator, people facing prosecution, including Fico's adviser and lawyer David Lindtner, helped write the amendments. On 17 January 2024 the European Parliament adopted a resolution (496–70–64) questioning Slovakia's ability to fight corruption and protect the EU budget, criticising the fast-track procedure and the dissolution of the office; the European Public Prosecutor's Office had warned that some changes could put the protection of EU financial interests at risk. President Zuzana Čaputová and opposition MPs challenged the law; in late February 2024 the Constitutional Court suspended all changes to the Penal Code and several changes to the Criminal Procedure Code, but not the abolition of the office, which ceased in March 2024. Fico then said that if he could, he would remove the court's president, Ivan Fiačan. On 3 July 2024 the court ruled the abolition of the office constitutional and upheld most of the suspended changes. A referendum initiated by petition on 4 July 2026 asking, among other things, whether the Special Prosecutor's Office and the National Crime Agency should be restored failed because turnout was 16.13%, far below the 50% threshold. In December 2025 parliament passed, again in a fast-track procedure, a further amendment to the Criminal Code and the Criminal Procedure Code that made evidence obtained from cooperating defendants (so-called kajúcnici, 'penitents') unusable in certain cases; coalition MPs argued the institution had been abused, for example in convictions based on testimony that proved unreliable. 51 opposition MPs, Prosecutor General Maroš Žilinka and the Specialised Criminal Court challenged it; the Constitutional Court suspended that provision in February 2026 and on 21 October 2026 ruled it unconstitutional, rejecting the rest of the petition (TASR).
key_facts: Amendments passed on 8 February 2024 by fast-track procedure
European Parliament resolution of 17 January 2024 (496 votes to 70, 64 abstentions)
Constitutional Court suspended parts in February 2024 and on 3 July 2024 upheld the abolition of the office and most changes
Referendum of 4 July 2026 on restoring the office invalid (turnout 16.13%)
Constitutional Court, 21 October 2026: the December 2025 provision making evidence from cooperating defendants (kajúcnici) unusable is unconstitutional; rest of the petition rejected

title: Replacement of public broadcaster RTVS by STVR (2024)
description: In 2024 the coalition replaced Radio and Television of Slovakia (RTVS) with a new public broadcaster, Slovak Television and Radio (STVR). Fico and Culture Minister Martina Šimkovičová (SNS) had repeatedly criticised RTVS as biased against them, but could not remove its director general, elected by the previous parliament for a term to 2027; dissolving the broadcaster allowed new management to be appointed. The law passed on 20 June 2024 with the votes of all 78 coalition MPs, while the opposition left the chamber, and STVR started on 1 July 2024 (dpa via blue News, ANSA). Tens of thousands of people had protested against the plan earlier in the year, and the European Parliament said in January 2024 that it was worried about the planned restructuring of RTVS.
key_facts: Law passed 20 June 2024 by 78 coalition MPs; opposition boycotted the vote
STVR replaced RTVS from 1 July 2024
Months of protests and criticism from journalists' groups and EU institutions

title: Lifetime pension for long-serving prime ministers ('lex atentát', 2024) and the failed 2026 referendum
description: After the May 2024 attempt on his life, Fico's government approved in June 2024 a package dubbed 'lex atentát', including limits on public gatherings and a lifetime monthly payment, equal to an MP's salary (€3,192 at the time), for prime ministers and speakers of parliament who have held office for at least twice the length of a presidential term (Act No. 166/2024, § 24a), which the Slovak Spectator described as two full electoral terms. According to the Slovak Spectator, only Fico meets the condition; he becomes entitled when he leaves office. A petition by the extra-parliamentary Demokrati party gathered more than 350,000 signatures, and President Peter Pellegrini called a referendum for 4 July 2026 asking whether to abolish the 'so-called lifetime rent, for example for Robert Fico' and whether to restore the Special Prosecutor's Office and the National Crime Agency, while refusing a question on early elections. Coalition leaders called the referendum politically motivated and did not campaign for it; turnout was 16.13%, so the result was invalid although more than nine in ten participants voted yes.
key_facts: June 2024: government approves 'lex atentát', including the lifetime payment
Payment equals an MP's salary; only Fico qualifies (Slovak Spectator)
4 July 2026 referendum invalid: turnout 16.13% (705,227 voters)

title: Visits to Vladimir Putin and attendance at Moscow and Beijing victory parades
description: On 22 December 2024 Fico met Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin, the third visit to Moscow by an EU head of government since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, amid his dispute with President Zelensky over the end of Russian gas transit through Ukraine (Euronews). Despite a warning by EU foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas that participation 'will not be taken lightly', Fico attended the 9 May 2025 Victory Day events in Moscow, saying: 'Nobody can order me where to go or not to go' and that he was honouring Red Army soldiers who liberated Slovakia (Euronews). On 2 September 2025 he met Putin again in Beijing and on 3 September attended China's military parade, the only leader of an EU member state to do so (Slovak Spectator). He returned to Moscow for the 9 May 2026 commemorations and was due to meet Putin; SaS leader Branislav Gröhling said he had 'once again betrayed Slovakia', while Fico said he was honouring the Soviet role in defeating fascism and described himself as the 'black sheep of the European Union'.
key_facts: 22 December 2024: talks with Putin in the Kremlin
9 May 2025: Moscow Victory Day events despite EU warnings
2–3 September 2025: meeting with Putin and military parade in Beijing
8–9 May 2026: second Victory Day visit to Moscow

title: Energy disputes with Ukraine and vetoes of EU sanctions (2025–2026)
description: After Ukraine let the Russian gas transit contract expire on 1 January 2025, Fico said Slovakia would lose about €500 million a year in transit fees and in a video message in early January 2025 threatened to cut financial aid for more than 130,000 Ukrainian refugees in Slovakia, saying Smer would also consider cutting electricity supplies to Ukraine (Euronews). In February 2026, when oil deliveries through the Druzhba pipeline stopped after what Kyiv said was a Russian drone strike, Fico called the halt 'a purely political decision to blackmail Slovakia', issued an ultimatum and on 23 February 2026 announced that Ukraine would no longer receive emergency electricity assistance; Ukraine's Foreign Ministry called the ultimatum 'blackmail' (Euronews; the Slovak Spectator reported that the cut-off appeared at that stage to be largely rhetorical). With Hungary, Slovakia blocked the EU's 20th sanctions package against Russia; Fico said in April 2026 that he would not agree to it 'unless there is a genuine reopening of the Druzhba oil pipeline', and lifted the veto once oil flows resumed later that month. An opposition criminal complaint against Fico over these decisions is listed in the justice section.
key_facts: January 2025: threat to cut refugee aid and electricity to Ukraine after gas transit ended
23 February 2026: emergency electricity assistance to Ukraine halted, according to Fico
20th EU sanctions package blocked by Slovakia and Hungary until Druzhba flows resumed in April 2026

title: Mass protests of 2024–2025 and Fico's claims of a planned coup
description: Protests that began after Fico's December 2024 visit to Moscow grew in January 2025, with up to 60,000 people in Bratislava on 24 January and rallies in dozens of towns (Al Jazeera). Fico, citing a secret report of the Slovak Information Service (SIS) presented to parliament, said organisers and the opposition were in contact with foreigners who had assisted protests in Ukraine in 2014 and Georgia in 2024 and planned to occupy government buildings, block roads and provoke clashes with police; on 23 January he called it 'an attempt to organise a typical coup in Slovakia' (Euronews). He did not present specific evidence; the organisers rejected the claims. The Security Council was convened and Smer added a Georgian commander of Ukraine's National Legion to a list of alleged threats; by April 2025, according to the Slovak Spectator, the protest organisers named by Fico said police had not contacted them and Fico had largely dropped the subject since early February.
key_facts: 24 January 2025: up to 60,000 protesters in Bratislava
Fico cited an SIS report and alleged a foreign-assisted coup plan
No evidence presented publicly; organisers not contacted by police as of April 2025

title: Reports linking Fico to a villa in Ražanj, Croatia
description: In March 2025 Croatian media reported that Fico had bought land and was building a summer house in the coastal village of Ražanj; Croatian newspapers found no construction or planning permits in his name. Fico wrote: 'Dear media, stop spreading yet another monstrous lie that I am building a villa in Croatia', adding that he would admit it if it were true. In July 2025 the Slovak Spectator, citing Aktuality.sk, reported that a villa in Ražanj repeatedly linked to Fico was listed for sale at about €1.15–1.19 million; it had first been registered to two young Slovaks with ties to Smer, who later said they had sold their shares. Fico denied owning the property but said in March 2025 that he planned to rent it for a holiday; local authorities said it was not registered as a legal rental. Opposition leader Igor Matovič alleges that the villa belongs to Fico through front men. No official ownership by Fico has been established and no proceedings have been reported.
key_facts: March 2025: Croatian media allegations; Fico denied building or buying property
July 2025: villa listed for about €1.19 million; ownership trail through Smer-linked Slovaks
No official record of Fico's ownership; Matovič's front-man allegation unproven

title: NGO law of 2025 and its annulment by the Constitutional Court
description: Fico campaigned in 2023 on bringing 'order' to non-governmental organisations; early drafts of the coalition's amendment would have labelled foreign-funded NGOs 'organisations with foreign support', and the coalition removed contested parts under EU pressure (STVR). The final law, passed on 16 April 2025 without the foreign-agent label and signed by President Pellegrini on 7 May 2025, required NGOs to file transparency reports, disclose donors and accept Interior Ministry oversight; critics called it a 'Russian law' and thousands protested, while Fico said it was 'European' in spirit (Slovak Spectator). In July 2025 the Constitutional Court rejected as 'false and unfounded' Fico's claim that foreign ambassadors had pressed its judges over the law, calling it an unacceptable interference with judicial independence. In mid-December 2025 the court found key parts of the law unconstitutional, including the mandatory publication of donors, warning that the rules could be used to harass NGOs; parliament did not amend it within six months and the law lost force on 4 August 2026 (SME, STVR). The coalition said it may return to the issue with a lobbying law.
key_facts: Passed 16 April 2025; signed 7 May 2025
July 2025: Constitutional Court rejected Fico's claims about ambassadors' visits
December 2025: key parts found unconstitutional; law lost force on 4 August 2026

title: Accusation that the United Kingdom interfered in the 2023 election
description: On 29 July 2025 Fico accused the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office of funding the London-based Zinc Network to run activities in Slovakia designed to 'damage Smer and help Progresívne Slovensko' before the 2023 election, calling it 'a targeted and deliberate act by a foreign power, our ally in NATO'; the British ambassador was summoned. The UK Foreign Office called the allegations 'completely untrue', saying the project encouraged young people to vote. Fico's claims drew on a Declassified UK report, which, according to the Slovak Spectator, did not mention the activists or journalists Fico referred to. On 30 March 2026 a police investigator rejected the case after an eight-month inquiry (Aktuality.sk via Slovak Spectator).
key_facts: 29 July 2025: accusation and summoning of the British ambassador
UK denied the claims
30 March 2026: police closed the inquiry with no case to answer

title: 2025 constitutional amendment on 'national identity' and EU infringement proceedings
description: On 26 September 2025 parliament adopted, with exactly the required 90 votes including some conservative opposition MPs, a constitutional amendment promoted by Fico as 'a dam against progressivism'. It states that there are only two sexes, male and female, restricts adoption almost exclusively to married couples, and provides that Slovakia retains sovereignty over matters of 'national identity', including cultural and ethical questions, over EU law (Al Jazeera). On 21 November 2025 the European Commission opened infringement proceedings with a letter of formal notice, saying the amended Article 7 allows Slovak authorities, including courts, to decide 'whether and to what extent Union law, including judgments of the Court of Justice, can be applied in Slovakia'. Fico had said on 7 November: 'We are looking forward to this conflict' (Anadolu). As of October 2026 no further stage of the proceedings was found in the sources consulted.
key_facts: 26 September 2025: amendment adopted with 90 of 150 votes
Two-sexes clause, adoption limits, 'national identity' sovereignty clause
21 November 2025: Commission letter of formal notice (infringement)

title: 'Chalk' protests and 'go to war' remark to students in Poprad (November 2025)
description: In early November 2025 a secondary-school student in Poprad wrote anti-Fico messages in chalk outside his school ahead of a planned visit by the Prime Minister and was taken from school by police for questioning the same day; Fico cancelled the visit, saying the two were unrelated. Chalk messages then appeared across Slovakia. At a discussion with students at the Poprad district office on 14 November 2025, after students in black began jingling keys, a gesture of the 1989 revolution, Fico said 'Well then, jingle away', and, according to the Slovak Spectator, told them to go to the front in Ukraine if they supported the war; the students walked out.
key_facts: Student questioned by police after chalk messages in Poprad
14 November 2025: students walked out of Fico's discussion
Chalk protest messages spread to many Slovak towns

title: Adviser Miroslav Lajčák's contacts with Jeffrey Epstein
description: Documents released in the United States from November 2025 showed extensive correspondence in 2017–2019 between Jeffrey Epstein and Miroslav Lajčák, Slovakia's foreign minister in all of Fico's earlier governments and his external adviser since April 2025. Opposition parties called for his dismissal; in December 2025 Fico defended him. After further messages, from 2018, were published in January 2026, Lajčák resigned on 31 January 2026, saying he wanted to spare the government political damage, condemning Epstein's conduct and denying taking part in or knowing of sexual encounters. Fico accepted the resignation and called him a 'great diplomat' and 'an incredible source of experience in diplomacy and foreign policy' (Slovak Spectator, Euronews). No proceedings against Lajčák were reported in the sources consulted.
key_facts: Lajčák: foreign minister in Fico's earlier governments, adviser from April 2025
Resigned 31 January 2026 after new Epstein messages were published
Fico defended him and called him a 'great diplomat'

title: Očistec (Purgatory) trial of former police president Tibor Gašpar, now a Smer MP
description: Tibor Gašpar, police president during Fico's governments (2012–2018) and now a Smer MP and deputy speaker of parliament, is a defendant in the Očistec (Purgatory) case. Prosecutors of the former Special Prosecutor's Office indicted the case in December 2021 on 20 counts, alleging that a group centred on Smer-linked businessman Norbert Bödör infiltrated the police and other institutions between 2012 and 2018 (founding and supporting a criminal group, bribery, abuse of office). The trial of eleven defendants, also including Bödör and former special prosecutor Dušan Kováčik, opened at the Specialised Criminal Court in Banská Bystrica on 11 May 2026, with 32 hearing dates scheduled until February 2027. The defendants deny wrongdoing. Fico has long described the case as evidence of politically motivated prosecutions after Smer lost power in 2020 (Slovak Spectator). Robert Fico is not a party to these proceedings; all defendants are presumed innocent.
key_facts: Indictment filed December 2021 (20 counts)
Trial opened 11 May 2026 at the Specialised Criminal Court; hearings scheduled to February 2027
Fico is not a party; he calls the case politically motivated

title: Arrests of former anti-crime investigators who had investigated Fico and his allies (2026)
description: On 3 March 2026 the Interior Ministry's police inspection service detained former members of the National Crime Agency (NAKA), the anti-corruption police unit dissolved by Fico's government in 2024, and a prosecutor; according to the Slovak Spectator, among them were officers who had investigated Fico and his allies. The inspection service said the case, opened in May 2025, concerns alleged manipulation of cases linked to the Takáč organised crime group in 2020 and earlier, and rejected claims that the detentions were linked to a press conference two days earlier at which Fico had criticised prosecutors, judges and former investigators and repeated that criminal law had been abused against him and Smer between 2020 and 2023. The supervising prosecutor's impartiality was questioned in the press. Fico is not a party to this case; those charged are presumed innocent.
key_facts: 3 March 2026: detentions by the police inspection service (ÚIS)
Case opened in May 2025; concerns events of 2020 and earlier
Followed Fico's press conference of 1 March 2026 criticising former investigators

title: Dismissal of Environment Minister Tomáš Taraba and the disputed nomination of his successor (2026)
description: After a months-long dispute between Environment Minister Tomáš Taraba and the SNS, which had nominated him, Fico submitted a proposal for Taraba's dismissal in mid-September 2026 and then withdrew it, which the SNS called a breach of the coalition agreement. On 29 September parliament passed a no-confidence motion against Taraba with 77 votes, from the opposition and almost all SNS MPs; on 30 September President Pellegrini dismissed him and entrusted Fico with running the ministry (TASR, prezident.sk). In mid-October Fico proposed SNS state secretary Filip Kuffa as minister. On 21 October 2026 Pellegrini asked Fico to reconsider, citing a criminal prosecution under way into suspected offences in organisations of the ministry, which he said could relate in part to Kuffa's work; Kuffa has not been charged and the President stressed the presumption of innocence. Fico said he was bound by the coalition agreement to propose the SNS chairman's nominee. As of 21 October 2026 Fico continued to run the ministry.
key_facts: 29 September 2026: no-confidence vote against Taraba (77 votes)
30 September 2026: Taraba dismissed; Fico entrusted with the Environment Ministry
21 October 2026: President asks Fico for a new nominee instead of Filip Kuffa
